meta.title: Check your understanding: The cost collapse

objectives: Describe how the price of a solar module fell between 1975 and 2024
Use Wright's law to estimate cost after a number of doublings of cumulative capacity
Explain why a steady percentage fall is a straight line on a logarithmic axis, and what drove the decline

questions.prompt: In Wright's law, known for solar modules as Swanson's law, what has to double for the cost to fall by one learning rate?
choices: Calendar time: the cost drops by that share every couple of years
The efficiency of the best laboratory cell
The number of factories making panels
The total capacity ever built, the cumulative capacity
questions.explain: The learning rate is the share of cost removed each time everything ever built doubles. Solar got cheap fast because the world kept doubling its cumulative capacity quickly, not because a fixed amount of time passed.

questions.prompt: A module costs $1.00 per watt when the world has built 100 GW in total. With a 20 % learning rate, what does Wright's law predict once 800 GW have been built?
questions.explain: 800 ÷ 100 = 8 = 2³, so n = 3 doublings and C = 1.00 × 0.8³ ≈ $0.51. Taking 20 % off three times is not 60 % off ($0.40), because each cut applies to the already lower price. Using 8 as the number of doublings gives 0.8⁸ ≈ $0.17.

questions.prompt: On the price chart each step down the vertical axis is ten times cheaper. What does a straight downward line on this chart mean?
choices: The price falls by the same percentage each year
The price falls by the same number of dollars each year
The price becomes ten times cheaper every year
questions.explain: On a logarithmic axis equal distances are equal ratios, so a steady percentage fall plots as a straight line. A fixed dollar drop each year would instead bend ever more steeply downward on these axes as the price neared zero.

questions.prompt: According to the studies the page cites, what drove the solar cost collapse?
choices: One breakthrough, the invention of the PERC cell in 1989
Cheaper silicon from new mines, with cell designs unchanged
Many causes adding up, with markets created by policy paying for factory scale
Research funding alone, rising steadily since the 1970s
questions.explain: No single invention did it: more efficient cells, thinner wafers and less silicon per watt, much bigger factories and steady research all added up. Public research mattered most early on; after about 2001, economies of scale in ever-larger factories became a bigger driver than research.
